summary: Defines SNMP management objects, written with SMIv2, for the interface attributes of the Integrated Services model. Operators can use them to inspect and configure how a device supports reservations.

eli5.summary: It is a settings panel that lets network operators read and change how a device handles reserved traffic.

questions: how to manage intserv with snmp
what is the integrated services mib
subtitle: SNMP objects for reading and configuring the reservation settings and active flows of Integrated Services devices.

tldr.problem: Devices that support Integrated Services reservations need a standard way for network managers to inspect and configure interface capacity and the flows being served.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module, written in SMIv2, with an interface attributes table and an interface flows table, plus compliance groups saying which objects a system must support.
tldr.outcome: Managers can read how much of an interface is reserved and can install, inspect or remove flow entries over SNMP, under rules that differ from a reservation negotiated with RSVP.

today: RFC 2213 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is written for SNMPv2 and SMIv2 and works with the Integrated Services services described in RFC 2212.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 2213 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the interface attributes defined in the Integrated Services model. It follows the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework, which has four components: the SMI for describing and naming objects, MIB-II as the core set of managed objects, the administrative architecture, and the protocol used to reach managed objects.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB. Each object type is defined in a subset of ASN.1 and named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name. An object type together with an instance identifies one specific instantiation.
sections.eli5: Network devices keep a big numbered list of things you can look at or change. This memo adds new entries to that list for reserved traffic.

sections.title: Structure and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module is named INTEGRATED-SERVICES-MIB and its root, intSrv, sits at { mib-2 52 }. Under it are four branches: objects, general objects, notifications and conformance. The MIB itself has two parts, the Interface Attributes Table and the Interface Flow Table.

Several new data types are introduced as textual conventions. They make the document easier to read but change neither syntax nor semantics, since each is encoded as the primitive type it is built on. They include SessionNumber (an identifier with no protocol meaning), Protocol (the IP protocol field, 1 to 255, such as 6 for TCP and 17 for UDP), SessionType (the RSVP session C-Type), Port, MessageSize, BitRate (bits per second), BurstSize (octets of IP data a stream may send without concern for policing) and QosService.

QosService names the class of service in use by a flow: bestEffort (1), guaranteedDelay (2) and controlledLoad (5).
sections.eli5: The memo makes up a few friendly names for kinds of numbers, like 'bits per second', so the list is easier to read. The numbers themselves are ordinary.

sections.title: Interface Attributes Table
sections.content:
The Integrated Services Interface Attributes Database holds information about resources allocated by reservation protocols such as RSVP and ST-II. It is a table indexed by ifIndex, with one row per interface and these columns:

  • intSrvIfAttribAllocatedBits: bits per second currently allocated to reserved sessions (read-only).
  • intSrvIfAttribMaxAllocatedBits: the most that may be allocated (read-create).
  • intSrvIfAttribAllocatedBuffer: buffer space needed to hold the simultaneous burst of all reserved flows (read-only).
  • intSrvIfAttribFlows: the number of active reserved flows, whether created by a reservation protocol or by configuration (read-only).
  • intSrvIfAttribPropagationDelay: extra delay in microseconds the interface adds beyond bit propagation, default 0 (read-create).
  • intSrvIfAttribStatus: a row status that is active on interfaces configured for RSVP.
sections.eli5: For each road, this page shows how much is already booked, how much may be booked at most, how many bookings there are, and any extra delay the road adds.

sections.title: Interface Flow Table
sections.content:
The Active Flows Database lists the flows active on an outgoing interface and their attributes. It is indexed by intSrvFlowNumber, a number used only for SNMP indexing. A manager creates a row using intSrvFlowNewIndex: read it, then write the value back in the SET that creates the row. If the SET fails with inconsistentValue, the process is repeated.

Each row identifies the session and its traffic. It includes the session type, the owner (other, rsvp or management), destination and sender addresses with their lengths in bits, the IP protocol, destination and source ports, the IPv6 flow ID (0 to 16777215), the interface and its address. A sender address of all zeroes means all senders, and these identifying objects cannot change while the row is active.

Other columns describe the service. intSrvFlowRate is the reserved rate: for Controlled Load it derives from the Tspec rate r, and for Guaranteed service from the Rspec rate R. intSrvFlowBurst is the largest expected burst, and intSrvFlowMinTU and intSrvFlowMaxTU are the minimum and maximum message sizes, the latter not exceeding the interface MTU. The weight and queue objects are implementation-specific. Counters intSrvFlowBestEffort and intSrvFlowPoliced count packets remanded to best effort and packets policed. intSrvFlowDiscard chooses whether policed traffic is lost (true) or treated as best effort (false, the default). intSrvFlowOrder sets the order a classifier tries rows, starting with 0. intSrvFlowStatus can install static classifier information, delete it or authorize it.
sections.eli5: This page is a list of every booking. Each line says who it is for, how fast a lane they get, how big a burst is allowed, and what happens to anyone who sends more than they promised.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
The module ends with compliance information. The compliance statement intSrvCompliance makes two groups mandatory: intSrvIfAttribGroup, covering the interface attributes, and intSrvFlowsGroup, covering the flow objects. Both groups are described as required for systems supporting the Integrated Services Architecture.

Many flow objects have their minimum access relaxed to read-only, so an implementation need not allow managers to create or change them. The flow ID object is needed only in a system that implements IPv6.
sections.eli5: A checklist says which pages a device must have to claim support. For many entries it is enough to let people look but not change them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo makes one specific point: using an SNMP SET results in an RSVP or Integrated Services reservation under rules that are different from those of a reservation negotiated with RSVP. Beyond that, it says no other security considerations exist other than those imposed by SNMP itself.
sections.eli5: If an operator writes a booking by hand, it is not checked the same way as one made through the normal booking process. Otherwise, the usual SNMP safety rules apply.
